content: 1. The research question or objective of the study was clearly stated. 2. The study population was clearly specified and well-defined. 3. The participation rate of eligible individuals was at least 50%. 4. All subjects were selected or recruited from the same or similar populations, including the same time period. Inclusion and exclusion criteria for study participation were pre-specified and applied uniformly to all participants. 5. A justification for the sample size, a description of statistical power, or estimates of variance and effect size were provided. 6. The exposures of interest were measured prior to the measurement of the outcomes. 7. The timeframe of the study was sufficient to reasonably expect an association between exposure and outcome, if one existed. 8. For exposures that could vary in amount or level, the study examined different levels of exposure in relation to the outcome (e.g., categories of exposure or exposure measured as a continuous variable). 9. The exposure measures (independent variables) were clearly defined, valid, reliable, and implemented consistently across all study participants. 10. The exposures were assessed more than once over time. 11. The outcome measures (dependent variables) were clearly defined, valid, reliable, and implemented consistently across all study participants. 12. The outcome assessors were blinded to the exposure status of the participants. 13. The loss to follow-up after baseline was 20% or less. 14. Key potential confounding variables were measured and statistically adjusted for their impact on the relationship between exposures and outcomes. For randomized controlled trials: The quality of random allocation concealment was assessed as adequate, uncertain, or inadequate. The comparability of groups at baseline was evaluated as comparable, not mentioned, or not comparable. The blinding of healthcare providers was assessed as stated, unclear, or not blinded. The blinding of outcome assessors to the intervention was evaluated as stated, unclear, or not blinded. The follow-up time was categorized as more than a year, less than a year, or no follow-up (assessment at the end of the trial). The percentage of follow-up at the end of the trial or follow-up period was categorized as 60% or more, 40-59%, or less than 40%. Details of dropouts were categorized as stating numbers and reasons for withdrawals, stating withdrawals only without numbers or reasons, or not mentioned. Validated outcome measures were categorized as used, unclear, or not used. Reporting of outcomes was categorized as measured objectively, self-reported, or not stated. Intention-to-treat analysis was categorized as performed, possibly performed but unclear, or not performed. The total quality score was calculated, with thresholds for strong (>15), moderate (10-15), and weak (<10) studies. For specific studies: Ferreira S (2014): A descriptive cross-sectional study nested within U-MDT CT/BR aimed to assess patient profiles and treatment satisfaction among paucibacillary leprosy patients. Data were collected via interviewer-led surveys, with 342 participants (268 MB, 74 PB). Statistical analysis included chi-squared tests and Mann-Whitney tests. Goncalves H (2012): A nested prospective study within U-MDT CT/BR aimed to assess adverse events. Newly diagnosed, untreated leprosy patients were enrolled, and data were collected from 2007-2008. U-MDT treatment included supervised and self-administered doses of rifampicin, dapsone, and clofazimine. Kroger A (2008): An open-field trial aimed to assess the side effects of U-MDT in leprosy patients from five centers in India and China. Patients were followed up for two years after treatment. Each study's follow-up details, dropout rates, and statistical analyses were documented, with quality ratings ranging from fair to good.
